passage: When I was in Class 10, I never really chose science. It chose me. I'm Karthik, and in our family everyone takes science: Appa, both my cousins Aditi and Ishita, even my uncle who now runs a bakery. Amma told the relatives her son would be an engineer too. When the stream form came, the science box was already ticked in my head. I loved history, the stories, the maps. My history teacher even asked if I'd thought about humanities. I said, "Maybe," and did nothing. Ticking a different box meant explaining myself at every Sunday lunch. It was easier to go along. Now, in Class 12, I sit in physics thinking about old kingdoms. I didn't decide. I just never decided otherwise.

qa.q: What subject did Karthik love?
qa.a: Karthik loved history, the stories and the maps.

qa.q: Why did Karthik do nothing after the history teacher's question?
qa.a: Choosing a different stream meant explaining himself to the whole family, so going along with science felt easier and safer than change.

qa.q: What could Karthik do now, in Class 12?
qa.a: He could talk to the history teacher about humanities options in college, so his next choice is made on purpose instead of by default.

qa.q: How might the history teacher feel seeing Karthik in physics?
qa.a: The teacher may feel a little sad, having noticed his love of history and hoped he would at least consider humanities.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy drifting into the family's usual stream because switching felt effortful, so the default became a choice he never made.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10 stream choices. Ritu ma'am.
Zubin came to me on the last day of the stream form deadline with commerce ticked. When I asked why, he said, "Abbu and both my brothers did commerce." I asked what he enjoys. His face changed; he talked for five minutes about the science fair and the water filter he built. When I asked if he had considered science, he said, "Switching would be a whole thing at home. Commerce is just... the normal one." He didn't seem unhappy, just carried along.
What I did: I gave him a one-page comparison of both streams to discuss at home, and extended his form deadline by two days.

qa.q: What did Zubin build for the science fair?
qa.a: Zubin built a water filter.

qa.q: Why did Zubin tick commerce even though his face lit up about science?
qa.a: Commerce is what Abbu and his brothers did, so it felt normal and safe; switching felt like a lot of trouble at home.

qa.q: Why was the counsellor's one-page comparison a good step?
qa.a: It turned the default into a real choice, giving Zubin something concrete to discuss at home and two more days to decide on purpose.

qa.q: How might Abbu react if Zubin brings the comparison home?
qa.a: Abbu might be surprised, since commerce seemed settled, but could be glad to hear about the water filter and his son's real interest.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy drifting into the stream his family chose because switching feels effortful, and a counsellor turning the default into a choice.

passage: In their small town near Rampur, everyone in Irfan's family had taken arts after Class 10: his father, the schoolteacher; his uncles; his sister Tanuja, now doing a B.A. Irfan, fifteen, spent his evenings at the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans. On the day the stream forms came, he ticked arts without thinking. "That's what we do," he said. Tanuja looked at the form, then at him. "Irfan, you fix phones for half the lane. You love circuits. Did you decide this, or did it just happen?" He shrugged. "Changing means talking to Abbu, and science is harder, and maybe I'll fail." "Maybe," Tanuja said. "Or maybe you'll love it. You haven't actually chosen anything yet." Their mother, Zeenat, called from the kitchen, "Talk to your Abbu tonight, beta. He'll listen." Irfan stared at the form for a long time. Then he picked up the eraser.

qa.a: At the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans.

qa.a: He picked up the eraser to rethink the form. Tanuja's question, whether he decided or it just happened, and Zeenat's encouragement helped him see he hadn't chosen yet.

passage: When I picked PCM in Class 11, I don't remember deciding. My father and both uncles were engineers, and the form at school already had PCM written in pencil by my name. I just traced over it in pen. My cousin Vidya-akka did the opposite: she spent a whole summer visiting colleges, sat in on a psychology class and picked humanities, even though the family argued for weeks. I thought she was making things hard for herself. Now, halfway through Class 12, she's glowing and I'm counting days. My father still calls me "our engineer Darshan," and I let him. I'm not even sure I'd have chosen differently. That's the strange part. I never gave myself the chance to find out.

passage:
School counsellor's note, stream-change window, Class 11
Sahil came in today because his friend Suraj had switched from science to arts last week and "looked so happy it was annoying." Sahil is in science because, as he put it, "everyone in my house did science, so I just did." When I asked what he would have chosen on a blank page, he said history, then laughed nervously. He listed reasons to stay: the tuition already paid, the group chat, the forms, what his mother would say. None of the reasons were about liking science. I told him the window closes on the 20th and that staying is also a choice he is allowed to make, as long as it is a choice. He will talk to his mother this weekend and come back on Monday.

qa.q: When does the stream-change window close?
qa.a: On the 20th.

qa.q: Why did Sahil laugh nervously after saying history?
qa.a: He felt nervous and a little exposed, because saying it out loud showed that science was a default he never truly chose.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Sahil?
qa.a: Asked what he would choose on a blank page, noticed his reasons weren't about liking science, and gave a clear deadline and next step.

qa.q: How does Suraj seem after switching?
qa.a: Suraj seems so happy that Sahil finds it annoying, which suggests the switch suited him.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage boy who is in the family's stream by default and has listed only effort-based reasons to stay.

Thursday

Stream forms are due tomorrow. Everyone in my family did science. Papa, Chacha, my two cousins. So I ticked science. It took one second.

Eshaan asked me at lunch, "Do you even like physics?" I said it's fine. Truth is, I like history and writing. I got my best marks in social studies. Eshaan is taking commerce even though his family is all doctors. He told his father straight. I don't know how he did that.

I'll probably just stay with science. It's easier.

— Chetan

His friend Lalit chose arts and told everyone he'd study psychology. Manoj felt a strange pinch. He liked biology; he spent hours reading about plants. He had just never said no.

passage:
In Pablo's family in Valencia, everyone had done the science track at secondary school. His father was an engineer. His mother, a pharmacist. His sister Clara was studying medicine.

When the time came to choose his subjects for the last two years, Pablo just ticked science. He didn't think about it much. It was what everyone did.

But in the evenings he drew. Comic strips, portraits, the old tram outside the window. His art teacher had said, twice, that he should consider the arts track.

One night Clara found his sketchbook. "Pablo, these are amazing. Why are you doing science?"

He shrugged. "It's what we do."

"Did you choose it, or did you just not choose anything else?"

Pablo stared at her. He had never actually thought about it.

"Switching feels like a lot of trouble," he admitted. "And what if it's a mistake?"

"What if staying is?"

qa.q: What did Pablo draw in the evenings?
qa.a: Comic strips, portraits, the old tram outside the window.

qa.q: Why did Pablo tick science without much thought?
qa.a: Pablo felt that switching would be effortful and risky, so following the family's default felt easier and safer.

qa.q: What small step could Pablo take after Clara's question?
qa.a: Pablo could talk to his art teacher and parents about the arts track, and look at what switching would really involve.

qa.q: How might Clara feel about Pablo's choice?
qa.a: Clara seems concerned and encouraging, wanting Pablo to actually choose rather than drift.

grounding: A teenager abroad drifts into the family's default science track because switching feels risky, though he loves art.

passage:
In the school counsellor's room, Santosh sat with his stream-selection form. Commerce was already ticked.

"Why commerce?" asked Nilesh sir, the counsellor.

"My father did commerce. My uncle did commerce. My brother's doing commerce."

"And what do you enjoy?"

Santosh hesitated. "Biology. I like the labs."

"Then why not science?"

"It's a lot of work to switch now. The forms, the tuition, explaining it at home. And what if I'm wrong?"

Nilesh sir nodded. "That's a real worry. But I want to check something. Did you choose commerce, or did commerce just happen?"

Santosh looked at the form. He hadn't really chosen anything. He had just not changed anything.

"Can I take the form home for a week?" he asked.

"Of course. And bring your parents in if you want. I'll help you talk it through."

qa.q: Which subject does Santosh enjoy?
qa.a: Biology. I like the labs.

qa.q: Why had Santosh ticked commerce without choosing it?
qa.a: Santosh felt that switching would be a lot of work and risk, so going with the family's default felt safer.

qa.q: How did Nilesh sir help Santosh without pushing?
qa.a: Nilesh sir asked whether Santosh chose commerce or it just happened, took the worry seriously and offered to help talk with the parents.

qa.q: How might Santosh's father react if Santosh chooses science?
qa.a: His father might be surprised at first, but may feel proud if Santosh explains his love for biology.

grounding: A teenager drifts into the family's default commerce stream because switching feels effortful and risky.

Dear Rajni ma'am,

You asked me after class why I seemed unhappy with my subjects. I didn't answer properly, so I'm writing.

I'm in PCM. My parents didn't force me. Everyone in my family did PCM, so when the form came, I just ticked it. It felt like the normal thing.

But I hate physics. What I love is history and geography. I read about old maps for fun.

I've thought about switching to humanities. But then I think of all the forms, and telling my parents, and my friends asking why. It feels so much easier to just stay.

When you asked me, I realised I never actually decided PCM. It just happened because I didn't decide anything else.

Could we talk about what switching would really involve? I'm scared, but I think I'd rather choose than drift.

Thank you,
Sahil

qa.q: What does Sahil love to read about for fun?
qa.a: I read about old maps for fun.

qa.q: Why did Sahil stay in PCM despite hating physics?
qa.a: Sahil felt that switching would be a hassle and a risk, so staying felt easier, and the default became a choice never really made.

qa.q: What step is Sahil taking, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sahil is asking Rajni ma'am to talk through what switching involves, which turns drifting into an actual decision.

qa.q: How might Rajni ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rajni ma'am may feel touched and glad Sahil trusted her, and ready to help.

grounding: A teenager realises the family's default stream was never really chosen and writes to a teacher about choosing instead.

passage: You want the honest answer, Zainab? Okay. It was Christmas break last year, the whole family at Nani's place in Goa, and someone asked which stream I'd picked. Before I could answer, Mausa said, "Science, obviously, like all of us." Everyone clapped. And I just nodded. Nobody forced me. The form was already on the table with PCM ticked, copied from my brother's old one, and changing it meant meeting the principal, convincing Papa, finding new tuition. It felt like climbing a hill for no reason. So I signed it. Now it's November, I'm in physics class drawing comics in the margins, and I keep thinking: I never actually chose this. It just happened to me. So yes, I'm Ojas, and that is the whole story of my big life decision. Don't laugh.
